articles.title: Professor pega bebê no colo para  aluna poder estudar no Acre; VÍDEO | G1
articles.standfirst: Natan Trindade é docente de espanhol da escola Lourival Pinho, em Rio Branco, e contou que situações como essas são comuns em sala de aula. Vídeo repercutiu nas redes sociais.
articles.summary: Natan Trindade é docente da escola Lourival Pinho, em Rio Branco, e contou que situações como essas são comuns em sala de aula. Vídeo repercutiu nas redes sociais nesta sexta (4).
articles.body:
O que começou como uma situação rotineira dentro de uma sala de aula acabou chamando a atenção nas redes sociais. O professor de espanhol Natan Trindade, da Escola Lourival Pinho, em Rio Branco , publicou um vídeo em que aparece com uma bebê no colo enquanto acompanha os alunos durante uma atividade. ( Assista acima )

A cena foi publicada nessa quinta-feira (3), durante o período de testes da escola. Ao g1 , o professor explicou que a criança é filha de uma das estudantes e que costuma ficar na sala durante as aulas. Os próprios alunos, inclusive, se revezam para cuidar dela enquanto a mãe estuda.

Para que os estudantes conseguissem concluir a atividade com mais tranquilidade naquele momento, o professor decidiu assumir o cuidado com a criança enquanto continuava acompanhando a turma.

"Para deixar os meninos mais à vontade de poder fazer a atividade tranquilamente, eu terminei de passar a atividade, coloquei a bebê no colo e fiquei circulando na sala, tirando as dúvidas", relembrou.

Natan Trindade é professor da rede pública do Acre desde o início deste ano — Foto: Reprodução

Natan tomou posse como professor em janeiro deste ano, mas já trabalha na educação desde 2019, quando atuava como assistente escolar na capital. Para ele, situações como essa fazem parte de uma realidade que nem sempre é percebida por quem está fora da escola.

Na escola, de acordo com o docente, há outras estudantes que são mães e também gestantes. Ele contou que atitudes como essa também fazem parte do processo de aprendizagem.

" Ensinar vai muito além de quadro, gramática, livros. Nós, enquanto professores, enquanto seres humanos, enquanto adultos, ensinamos com nossos gestos, com nossas palavras, com nossa atenção. Aquele momento foi uma ajuda pontual, mas também para que os alunos possam ter um pouco mais de empatia, de cuidado com o outro ", frisou.

A situação também ganhou outro significado para Natan por envolver mães adolescentes, que, segundo ele, muitas vezes retornam à escola com receio do julgamento dos colegas.

"Essas mães na adolescência, essas grávidas na adolescência, elas são muito julgadas, atacadas [...] eu trago para perto de mim, cuido, acolho, e é um trabalho da escola no geral que apoia as mães, que acolhe. Os outros professores também fazem isso de pegar, de cuidar", comentou.

📊 Segundo a última pesquisa do Instituto Brasileiro de Geografia e Estatística (IBGE) sobre gravidez na adolescência, divulgado em maio do ano passado, o Acre é o estado brasileiro com o maior percentual de mães até os 19 anos em 2023 , com 21,4% . Em termos estatísticos, uma em cada cinco mães no Acre tinha até 19 anos na data do parto do ano estudado.

Natan Trindade segurava filha de aluna para ela poder estudar; ato repercutiu nas redes sociais — Foto: Reprodução

Natan costuma publicar nas redes sociais registros do cotidiano escolar. A intenção, segundo ele, é mostrar que a rotina de uma escola envolve situações que vão muito além da transmissão de conteúdo.

"Algumas pessoas não têm noção do que é o dia a dia da escola. A escola não é só livro , não é só estudar. Nós trabalhamos com pessoas, com seres humanos, com vidas, e a nossa comunidade é periférica. Nós temos muitos alunos carentes, e às vezes as pessoas que estão de fora não têm noção do que é uma sala de aula", destacou.

Para o professor, a rotina de quem trabalha em sala de aula exige adaptação constante . Foi nesse contexto que publicou o vídeo com a bebê. A repercussão, no entanto, não era esperada.

"Todo dia é uma emoção diferente. Nós, professores, temos que nos inventarmos todos os dias. A gente chega preparado para uma coisa e tudo pode acontecer dentro da sala de aula, inclusive nada. E esse dia foi um dia em que a bebê tava lá e eu peguei para cuidar e todos os outros professores também tem esse mesmo cuidado não só com ela, mas com as outras que têm bebê também", falou.

Apesar da experiência cotidiana da equipe, Natan reconhece que as escolas ainda não estão necessariamente preparadas para receber estudantes adolescentes que chegam às aulas acompanhadas dos filhos.

Ele considerou que, na prática, professores, coordenação e direção acabam construindo soluções conforme as situações aparecem, a fim de evitar que as mães adolescentes abandonem os estudos por constrangimento ou falta de apoio.

"As mães voltam para a escola com muita vergonha de chegar com o bebê no colo, e aí nós, enquanto escola, enquanto professores, temos que ter esse olhar mais carinhoso, mais delicado de acolher, abraçar, receber e tratar da melhor forma", salientou.

Para Natan, o episódio que repercutiu acabou mostrando justamente uma realidade onde professores precisam lidar com diferentes situações em sala de aula enquanto tentam garantir que os estudantes continuem aprendendo.

"Na primeira vez que a gente chega e dá de cara com um adolescente com o bebê no colo, dentro de uma sala de aula com 35, 40 alunos, é um pouco desesperador. Mas nada que um coração valente e muito amor não resolva essa situação", finalizou.

articles.title: Entregador viraliza ao comparar tratamento que recebe no Rio e em SP | G1
articles.standfirst: João Victor de Sousa, de 25 anos, trabalha com entregas desde 2020 e afirma que clientes paulistanos costumam tratá-lo bem; vídeo publicado por ele sobre diferenças entre São Paulo e Rio de Janeiro viralizou nas redes sociais.
articles.summary: João Victor de Sousa, de 25 anos, trabalha com entregas desde 2020 e afirma que clientes paulistanos costumam tratá-lo bem; vídeo publicado por ele sobre diferenças entre São Paulo e Rio de Janeiro viralizou nas redes sociais.
articles.body:
Entregador João Victor trabalhou em São Paulo e no Rio de Janeiro para comparar as diferenças de tratamento entre uma cidade e outra — Foto: Reprodução/Instagram

Um vídeo que mostra diferenças no comportamento de clientes durante entregas por aplicativo viralizou nas redes sociais e reacendeu o debate sobre a relação entre consumidores e entregadores e, de quebra, a rivalidade entre paulistanos e cariocas.

O vídeo publicado há um dia já soma mais de 1 milhão de visualizações, 8,9 mil comentários e mais de 1.800 compartilhamentos. Autor da publicação, o entregador e criador de conteúdo João Victor de Sousa , de 25 anos, afirmou, em entrevista ao g1 , que, na capital paulista, costuma ser recebido sem confusões e elogiou o comportamento dos moradores da cidade. No Rio, onde mora, não é bem assim.

O profissional começou a atuar na área em 2020, durante a pandemia. Ele também produz vídeos de motovlog sobre a rotina de quem trabalha com entregas e atualmente acumula 280 mil seguidores no Instagram, no perfil "110i_joao".

Segundo ele, a principal diferença que percebe entre as entregas feitas no Rio de Janeiro e em São Paulo está na forma como os clientes recebem os pedidos.

"Em todas as entregas que eu fiz em São Paulo o cliente já estava na porta me aguardando. No Rio, de 50 entregas que eu faço, 20 arrumam confusão, porque querem que eu suba [até o apartamento]. Em São Paulo é o contrário, fui super bem tratado por todos os clientes e por todos os donos de loja também. As pessoas são muito mais educadas", afirmou.

Em resposta a um dos comentários na publicação, João Victor também fez questão de explicar que, para ele, a comparação apresentada no vídeo não tinha como objetivo classificar quem é mais ou menos educado . "É sobre o cliente descer e não reclamar com o motoboy."

Na primeira parte do vídeo, gravada no Rio, ele aparece em situações de conflito com moradores, que discutem com João Victor por interfone, alegando que não querem descer para buscar as encomendas, ou pessoalmente.

Em um dos trechos, uma cliente afirma que, segundo a propaganda do aplicativo, a entrega deveria ser feita "em casa". Outro morador reclama que "o trabalho é pela metade", enquanto um terceiro questiona por que o entregador não sobe até o apartamento.

"Quando o cliente se nega a descer para receber o pedido, eu aciono o suporte da plataforma que eu trabalho, e eles me protegem disso. Eu não sofro nenhuma penalidade. Às vezes, tenho que voltar para a loja e devolver o pedido e às vezes eu fico com o pedido. Enquanto isso eu fico protegido pela plataforma, porque ela recomenda que a entrega seja feita no primeiro ponto de encontro", contou.

O entregador afirma que a situação mais abusiva que enfrentou nos últimos anos ocorreu em São Francisco, Niterói.

"O cliente me xingou de tudo quanto é nome. A solução que eu encontrei foi acionar o suporte do iFood, fiz uma reclamação, mas não sei o que aconteceu, não sei se ele ainda continua ativo na plataforma fazendo pedidos, mas foi o caso mais abusivo que eu sofri."

Já nas imagens feitas em São Paulo, os clientes aparecem aguardando os pedidos no portão ou na calçada antes mesmo da chegada do motoboy. Eles conferem o código de validação e encerram o atendimento com cumprimentos e agradecimentos. Para João Victor, essa rotina faz a diferença na rotina exaustiva de trabalho.

Apesar disso, ele guarda uma situação de gentileza ocorrida em Niterói, entre as muitas experiências vividas durante o trabalho.

"Eu já recebi uma sobremesa de uma cliente. Ela pediu três açaís: deu um para mim, um para o porteiro e um ficou para ela. Era um dia de muito calor, ela foi muito gentil", completa.

A publicação do vídeo gerou milhares de comentários de usuários que relataram experiências pessoais com entregas no Rio de Janeiro e em São Paulo.

"Sou carioca e espero no portão, gente sem educação tem em todo lugar", escreveu um.

Uma carioca que mora em São Paulo há quatro anos disse ter se adaptado à rotina paulistana e defendeu que os clientes recebam os pedidos na entrada dos prédios.

"O motoboy/entregador não tem obrigação alguma de subir. Ele está no corre dele e precisa trabalhar. Para a segurança dele e também a nossa, a entrega é na porta do prédio."

As plataformas de entrega estabelecem orientações sobre o local em que os pedidos devem ser entregues e sobre o que deve ocorrer quando o cliente não aparece para recebê-los.

No iFood, a orientação oficial é que o entregador não precisa subir até a unidade nem entrar em condomínios. O pedido deve ser deixado no primeiro ponto de acesso do endereço informado no aplicativo. O cliente tem até 10 minutos, a partir da chegada do entregador, para retirá-lo.

“A obrigação do entregador é entregar no primeiro ponto de contato que existe na residência da pessoa. Se for no condomínio, esse ponto é a portaria. Essa é a recomendação dada para os entregadores e a comunicação passada para os consumidores”, explica Diego Barreto, CEO do iFood.

A empresa afirma ainda que descer para receber o pedido traz mais segurança para clientes e entregadores e agiliza o serviço.

A 99 Food não respondeu aos questionamentos sobre quais são as normas da empresa de aplicativo em casos de clientes que se recusam a ir de encontro ao entregador para receber a encomenda.

No ícone de política de privacidade do aplicativo, consta a informação de que o entregador, assim como nas demais empresas consultadas, deve aguardar até 10 minutos no local quando houver dificuldade para localizar quem vai receber o pedido. Caso ninguém apareça, o profissional deve voltar ao ponto de coleta e comunicar o ocorrido pelo chat. Depois disso, ele recebe um código para encerrar a corrida.

Não há nenhuma menção, porém, sobre onde deve ser feita a entrega.

A Keeta, por sua vez, não detalha em seus Termos de Serviço uma regra específica sobre subir ou não em prédios por não atuar no Rio de Janeiro , onde o hábito ainda é aplicado. No entanto, na política de segurança da empresa fica estabelecido o mesmo prazo de 10 minutos para que o entregador ou o suporte consiga contato com o cliente após a chegada ao endereço.

Depois desse período, o pedido é considerado entregue, e a empresa se isenta de responsabilidade por reembolso ou reenvio.

Em nota, a Keeta reforçou: "Os entregadores parceiros da plataforma não são obrigados a subir até a porta do apartamento do cliente, salvo casos excepcionais previstos por lei".

articles.standfirst: Com mais visitantes no verão, região amplia a pressão sobre água, saneamento e ambientes naturais ao mesmo tempo em que enfrenta eventos extremos e transformações na zona costeira
articles.summary: O aumento de turistas na Baixada Santista pressiona o saneamento e o abastecimento de água, enquanto eventos climáticos extremos ameaçam a infraestrutura e os ecossistemas da região.
articles.body:
Receber mais turistas na alta temporada movimenta hotéis, restaurantes e o comércio, mas também coloca à prova estruturas dimensionadas para uma população menor. No litoral de São Paulo, esse aumento coincide com um período marcado por ondas de calor, chuvas intensas e ressacas.

Meses depois, em julho e agosto, rajadas superiores a 100 km/h interromperam temporariamente as operações no Porto de Santos e as travessias de balsas, provocando ocorrências em diferentes municípios.

Para o pesquisador e professor Ronaldo Christofoletti , do Instituto do Mar da Unifesp, a relação precisa ser observada nos dois sentidos. O turismo amplia a pressão sobre os recursos e a infraestrutura , enquanto as mudanças climáticas podem modificar as próprias condições que ajudaram a consolidar a região como destino turístico.

"O nosso turismo, da forma como se consolidou, baseou-se no clima das últimas décadas. No entanto, o clima mudou ", afirmou Ronaldo ao g1.

Centro de Santos teve estruturas destruídas após a ventania. — Foto: Reprodução e Matheus Croce/TV Tribuna

A importância econômica desse movimento reflete-se nos números do setor. Segundo o Sindicato de Hotéis, Restaurantes, Bares e Similares da Baixada Santista e Vale do Ribeira (Sinhores) , a movimentação cresce, em média, cerca de 40% ao longo do ano.

Em feriados prolongados e na alta temporada, o aumento pode variar entre 70% e 80% , com a ocupação hoteleira próxima de 100% nas festas de dezembro .

Ao g1 , o secretário de Fomento Turístico do Sinhores, Kauê Lima , destacou que o fluxo beneficia a rede de serviços e contribui significativamente para o aquecimento da economia local .

Veículos seguem em direção à Baixada Santista. — Foto: Luigi Bongiovanni/AT

O impacto, contudo, acaba se refletindo no consumo de água. A Sabesp informou a reportagem que a demanda cresce, em média, 30% no verão, principalmente entre o Natal e o Ano Novo . Na última temporada, o litoral paulista recebeu cerca de 30% mais pessoas nas festas em comparação com a média da década anterior.

Os maiores acréscimos médios de consumo registrados nos últimos anos foram:

Para lidar com os picos , a concessionária reforçou em 40% as equipes de plantão no último período de festas e utilizou dezenas de caminhões-pipa em áreas mais críticas .

Entre 29 de dezembro de 2025 e 3 de janeiro de 2026, foram entregues mais de 12 milhões de litros de água por esse sistema. A companhia também afirma ter investido R$ 2,4 bilhões na região desde julho de 2024 e prevê outros R$ 8,1 bilhões entre 2026 e 2029.

A empresa de saneamento explicou que temperaturas elevadas, estiagens e chuvas irregulares também interferem na operação . Em 2025, os baixos índices pluviométricos reduziram a vazão dos rios, enquanto temporais levaram lama, terra e detritos aos pontos de captação, comprometendo temporariamente o tratamento.

O saneamento básico é outro gargalo. Mais pessoas significam maior produção de esgoto e, quando a infraestrutura não acompanha os picos de demanda, aumentam os riscos de impactos sobre rios, canais e praias .

Imagens da captação de água no rio Mambú, da estação de tratamento de água (ETA) Mambú/Branco — Foto: Divulgação/Sabesp

Eventos extremos colocam o turismo à prova

Uma ocorrência que já representa um desafio para os moradores ganha outra dimensão quando a cidade recebe uma população muito maior que a habitual.

"Lidar com isso em uma cidade de 600 mil habitantes é uma coisa; com 2 milhões de pessoas, é outra", exemplificou Ronaldo.

As ondas de calor afetam diretamente a experiência dos turistas, aumentando o desgaste físico e o desconforto. A combinação entre temperaturas extremas e aglomerações também pode ampliar riscos sanitários. “Teremos cada vez mais surtos de viroses e infecções bacterianas” , disse o pesquisador.

Chuvas intensas , por sua vez, comprometem deslocamentos, provocam alagamentos e ampliam a exposição a situações de risco . Para quem não conhece a geografia local, identificar áreas vulneráveis e saber como agir diante de uma emergência torna-se ainda mais difícil.

O setor turístico , por outro lado, não vê hoje um cenário de perda da atratividade regional . Kauê Lima acrescentou que a proximidade com a capital, a diversidade de atrativos e a estrutura de serviços sustentam a atividade ao longo do ano.

"Na avaliação do setor, embora as condições climáticas exijam atenção e planejamento, a tendência é que eventuais impactos sejam temporários, sem comprometer a atratividade da região no médio e longo prazo" avaliou o representante do Sinhores.

A preocupação do pesquisador da Unifesp, contudo, aponta para outro horizonte. Erosão, ressacas e alterações ambientais podem modificar as praias , criando impactos diretos sobre negócios que dependem desses espaços.

"Se uma orla sofre forte erosão devido às ressacas e à elevação do nível do mar, ela pode receber menos visitantes. O que acontece com a economia local, os barraqueiros, os ambulantes, as pousadas e os restaurantes que dependem diretamente daquela faixa de areia? ", questionou.

Erosão nas praias de São Vicente preocupam autoridades — Foto: Carlos Abelha/TV Tribuna

Segundo o biólogo marinho Jorge Luis dos Santos , o alerta não se restringe à faixa de areia. O pesquisador explicou ao g1 que o aumento sazonal do público agrava problemas que já ocorrem no restante do ano , principalmente relacionados ao lixo e ao esgoto.

Durante a alta temporada, a quantidade de resíduos pode superar a capacidade de recolhimento das prefeituras . O material acaba acumulado em espaços públicos e chega aos rios e ao oceano, afetando a vida marinha . O despejo irregular de esgoto também piora com o contingente extra.

"A poluição por esgoto somada ao lixo é, sem dúvida, o maior problema ambiental relacionado ao turismo em massa ", cravou o especialista.

Rio dos Bugres, na região estuarina entre Santos (SP) e São Vicente (SP) — Foto: William Rodriguez Schepis

Praias arenosas, costões rochosos, restingas e manguezais estão entre os ambientes mais sensíveis. Além da poluição, esses locais sofrem com a circulação de embarcações turísticas, especialmente nas áreas próximas aos manguezais . A conservação desses espaços também ajuda a proteger o litoral, já que manguezais e dunas funcionam como barreiras naturais contra o avanço das águas oceânicas.

🚤 O movimento das embarcações gera ondas que desgastam as margens, derrubam árvores de mangue e podem destruir ninhos marinhos. Âncoras, motores e vazamentos de óleo também danificam os costões e afetam a fauna local

A balneabilidade da água do mar também é impactada pela combinação de fatores. A Cetesb explicou que o principal indicador medido é a presença de enterococos (bactérias que apontam contaminação fecal). A proliferação desses microrganismos pode estar ligada a extravasamentos, ligações irregulares e ao transporte de poluentes pelas chuvas.

Na Baixada Santista, áreas próximas a rios, estuários e manguezais são mais sensíveis porque recebem diretamente a influência das bacias de drenagem. Em períodos de chuva intensa, a drenagem urbana e os cursos d’água podem carregar poluentes para o mar, pressionando ainda mais a qualidade das praias.

Santos sofre pressões relacionadas à urbanização, às atividades portuárias e industriais e à perda de áreas de manguezal — Foto: Marcelo Justo/Acervo A Tribuna

A Secretaria de Meio Ambiente, Infraestrutura e Logística (Semil) informou ao g1 que as projeções para São Paulo indicam elevação da temperatura, maior duração de ondas de calor e possível intensificação de chuvas extremas , com potenciais reflexos em inundações, deslizamentos e erosão.

Na Baixada Santista, os estudos apontam a região entre as áreas que podem ser mais afetadas por eventos climáticos extremos e processos erosivos. A Semil ressalta que, embora os estudos não façam projeções específicas para o turismo nem avaliem a elevação do nível do mar, os efeitos previstos ameaçam a infraestrutura, os ecossistemas e as atividades econômicas locais .

Uma das respostas do poder público está no controle da visitação. Segundo o órgão ambiental, as Unidades de Conservação estaduais da Baixada Santista recebem de 300 mil a 500 mil pessoas por ano , com até 70% desse público concentrado entre dezembro e março . Para evitar que o fluxo ultrapasse a capacidade de suporte da natureza, a Fundação Florestal desenvolve estudos incorporados aos Planos de Manejo .

Esses documentos estabelecem limites de acesso a atrativos ecológicos (trilhas, cachoeiras e mirantes) e consideram impactos que vão desde a compactação do solo e a poluição de rios até o afugentamento da fauna. Os Planos de Manejo também definem zonas de uso, separando as faixas de ecoturismo regulado daquelas de proteção integral.

O planejamento abrange, ainda, situações de risco. O órgão estadual mantém sinalização em áreas vulneráveis e protocolos para a retirada de visitantes diante de mudanças bruscas no tempo. Além disso, as trilhas recebem estruturas de baixo impacto (como deques e passarelas) que reduzem o pisoteio direto, preservam a vegetação e contêm a degradação do terreno.

Visitante desce a tirolesa Voo da Serra, no parque Caminhos do Mar. Atração corta a Mata Atlântica com vista para a Baixada Santista — Foto: Fábio Tito/g1

Por meio do programa Monitora Bio SP , a fauna e a flora são acompanhadas com "armadilhas fotográficas" e amostragens de campo . Simultaneamente, moradores de comunidades tradicionais são capacitados como guias para atuar no entorno das áreas protegidas e auxiliar na organização turística.

A Semil destaca que as ações de planejamento territorial, conservação, monitoramento ambiental e gestão das Unidades de Conservação são desenvolvidas de forma permanente, com o objetivo de conciliar a proteção dos recursos naturais com o uso público ordenado dos espaços protegidos.

articles.title: Top military officials faced polygraphs over leaks on munitions, sources say
articles.summary: Some of the highest-ranking officials in the U.S. military were subjected to polygraph tests as part of a sweeping leak probe, U.S. officials briefed on the...
articles.body:
Washington — Some of the highest-ranking officials in the U.S. military were subjected to polygraph tests as part of a sweeping leak probe after highly sensitive classified details about the nation's stockpiles of sophisticated weapons were reported in the media, U.S. officials briefed on the matter told CBS News.

President Trump was furious about the leaks, according to three of the sources, who spoke on condition of anonymity. A very small set of people had access to the classified details on the munitions, and there was concern about whether anyone could potentially be acting as a foreign intelligence asset, one of the sources said.

Polygraph tests are often a part of the routine cadence for top military and civilian officials, but the mass volume of people who were pulled in for testing in this case was extremely rare, officials said.

Several dozen people were given the tests earlier this summer, including some U.S. Central Command officials as well as other combatant commanders.

The polygraph questions delved deeply into various national security-related matters. No one failed the questions meant to determine if these officials leaked to the media, two of the sources said.

Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said in a statement to CBS News on Friday night: "The Department does not comment on internal personnel or investigative matters but takes all leaks of classified national security information extremely seriously and investigates accordingly. Securing classified information is critical to ensuring the security of the United States and of our troops deployed around the world."

Not all senior military officials were part of the testing. For example, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, Gen. Dan Caine, wasn't polygraphed, a senior Pentagon official said.

The New York Times was first to report on the polygraph tests.

Weeks into the Iran war, CBS News and other news outlets had reported information concerning the rapid pace at which the U.S. was expending some of its most advanced finite munitions.

In July, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced the Pentagon and Justice Department had formed a joint task force to identify and prosecute people suspected of leaking sensitive government information to the press, significantly expanding an effort that had begun inside his own office.

Hegseth gave the Pentagon's Office of General Counsel, led by Earl Matthews, broad authority to demand information, records and assistance for leak investigation. Pentagon officials and personnel were instructed to prioritize those requests and respond within a two-day period.

"When a leak of department information occurs today, it's critical that we provide the Department of Justice and other partners in federal law enforcement — including the FBI — with actionable information as quickly as possible," Hegseth said when he announced the task force.

He added: "Leaked information risks lives."

The move came days after the Justice Department subpoenaed several New York Times reporters over their reporting on security shortcomings aboard Mr. Trump's new Qatari-donated Air Force One.

Later, the Justice Department withdrew its subpoenas for grand jury testimony and phone records. The decision followed a contentious court hearing where a U.S. district judge grilled federal prosecutors on why they had issued the subpoenas before taking further investigative steps, according to previous CBS News reporting.

Polygraphs aren't unusual for government officials who have permission to view top-secret files or "special access programs," which place even tighter controls on sensitive national security information. Tests are given every few years to recertify an individual's clearance.

The scope of the testing this summer indicates an investigation, national security officials told CBS News. The FBI was not involved in these polygraph tests, several people with direct knowledge of the matter said.

Secretaries of defense have the authority to direct counterintelligence investigations that can include polygraph examinations, but federal law and Pentagon regulations also impose restrictions on when polygraphs may be used and require procedural safeguards. In those circumstances, the person being examined must consent to or request the test.

That includes cases in which investigators are trying to resolve serious information uncovered during a security investigation or when someone wants to clear themselves of allegations or evidence that emerged during an investigation.

Under federal law , a defense secretary is required to ensure that polygraph examinations are used in a "responsible and effective" manner within the Defense Department and is also required to provide information to congressional bodies on polygraph use.

For Hegseth, the latest effort is not the first time he has turned to polygraphs amid concerns about leaks from inside the Pentagon.

Following the ouster of Gen. C.Q. Brown, the former chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, Hegseth was reportedly furious last year after details of a planned classified briefing on China set up for Elon Musk at the Pentagon had leaked to the press, according to The Wall Street Journal .

The newspaper reported that Hegseth shouted at Adm. Christopher Grady, the then-acting Joint Chiefs chairman, and demanded evidence he wasn't the source for leaking the March 21, 2025, briefing. Citing two anonymous people familiar with the exchange, the newspaper said Hegseth yelled at Grady: "I'll hook you up to a f—ing polygraph!"

The Journal reported Grady was never subjected to a polygraph examination as Hegseth accused others of leaking, including Lt. Gen. Doug Sims, who served as director of the Joint Staff and was also threatened with a polygraph.

Hegseth decided against promoting Sims to four-star general, the Times reported. He retired last September.

articles.title: Illinois mother charged with murder after killing 2-year-old, attempting to harm herself
articles.summary: A suburban Illinois mother, who had become interested in the Lindsay Clancy case, has been charged with murder after she allegedly killed her 2-year-old son...
articles.body:
A suburban Illinois mother, who had become interested in the Lindsay Clancy case , has been charged with murder after she allegedly killed her 2-year-old son then attempted to harm herself, according to police and court records.

A quiet street in the affluent village of Frankfort, Illinois, about 35 miles southwest of Chicago, became a scene of terror earlier this week when the 2-year-old child was found hanging in the basement and his mother, Corie A. Walsh, was discovered in a bathtub in an apparent suicide attempt.

Walsh, 40, was charged with three counts of first-degree murder on Friday, police announced.

Before the killing, Walsh had "recently become very invested in the Lindsay Clancy murder trial," prosecutors said in their petition to deny her pretrial release.

Clancy, who was accused of murdering her three children in January 2023, has been in the national spotlight the last few weeks as her trial was live-streamed. It culminated in a mistrial Friday.

Walsh had been "actively discussing the case" in group text messages with her friends up until 12:30 p.m. Tuesday — just three and a half hours before the grisly scene at her home was discovered, the filing said. At the time in the trial, the jury was in deliberations.

Frankfort police had responded to the home just after 4 p.m. Tuesday on a report of an unresponsive child, authorities said .

When officers arrived they found a neighbor performing CPR on the toddler, Barrett Walsh, who she had found hanging in the basement, court documents said.

The neighbor took the child down and attempted CPR while calling 911, but he was already cold with no pulse, prosecutors said.

The child was transported to a local hospital, where he was pronounced deceased. The Will County Coroner's Office ruled his death as an apparent homicide. Preliminary findings of the autopsy say he died from asphyxia due to ligature compression of the neck, the petition said.

Officers found Walsh in the bathroom of the upstairs master bedroom, laying in a tub fully dressed and "surrounded by bloody water." Walsh was found with cuts to her wrists and thighs, the petition said. She was taken to a hospital with non-life-threatening injuries, police said.

Walsh told officers "she did this to her baby because he was the 'devil' and the 'anti-Christ,'" the filing said.

The neighbor told officers she had found Walsh with a knife in her hands, "actively harming herself." The neighbor took the knife and threw it into the sink, and it was later taken into evidence, according to the petition.

After she took the knife away, Walsh asked her why she did that, " as she was trying to kill herself," the petition said.

Walsh then told the neighbor that "Bear," the child's nickname, was "in the basement," the filing said.

Police on Wednesday said that the preliminary investigation indicated it was a domestic-related homicide.

Walsh's husband was out of town at the time. An infant was home and unharmed, prosecutors said.

Two school-aged children had returned home around the time Barrett was found and they were also physically unharmed, the filing said.

Walsh allegedly made statements regarding harming her other children and statements that she intended to harm her husband upon his return home, prosecutors said in the filing.

Once hospitalized, she also described to officers "the manner in which she killed Barrett," which was consistent with evidence at the scene, the petition said.

Walsh was in custody Friday night and being held for medical treatment. Once released, she'll be transferred to the Will County Adult Detention Facility.

It was not immediately clear whether she has retained an attorney.

Frankfort police called the case a "heartbreaking tragedy," saying, "We ask our community to keep them in their thoughts and prayers."

articles.title: I was real target of Jantar Mantar attacker, says Class X student
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: A Class X student whose short videos went viral during Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) protests said Friday she was the original target of a gr.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: A Class X student whose short videos went viral during Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) protests said Friday she was the original target of a group that had come armed with sticks to Jantar Mantar.Speaking to TOI Friday after a CJP team protested at Parliament Street police station and demanded an FIR against Swatantra Bhardwaj, who claimed responsibility for an attack on her father, she said it was ironical that her demand for justice was met after the alleged attacker had bragged on a video about it. TOI is withholding her name because she is a minor.The student, who identifies herself as an Ambedkarite influencer, started her YouTube channel in 2023 and runs an Instagram account with the same name. Her videos capturing reactions of students affected by paper leaks and delayed recruitment exams and demanding accountability resonated widely. During the CJP protests, her channel became a key source for online updates about the Jantar Mantar.Alleging she had faced abuse online and was hounded for speaking up, she said questions directed at her since Bhardwaj’s video surfaced online were about the injuries her father had suffered, instead of whether she had got justice.“It’s sad that I have to justify my father’s injuries to people because police keep calling it a ‘simple injury’,” she said. Describing the attack on her father on June 23, she added, “Some people came with the intention of attacking me at night, but my father and others shielded me. Later, the same people came again and attacked my father with a kada (thick metal bangle) and my father’s skull cracked open. He was bleeding profusely.”The next day, she alleged, she saw the men – among them Bhardwaj who she didn’t know by name then – roaming freely at the protest site at the same spot where they attacked her father. She also posted a video of the same on her Instagram handle. After the attack, she stood on the dais alongside CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke and requested the authorities for speedy justice.Recently, a video surfaced in which Bhardwaj claimed nothing could happen to him. In the clip, Bhardwaj is seen saying he “cracked open the skull” of the influencer's father because he did not like what his daughter was doing at the protest and on her YouTube channel.“The question should not be how badly my father was injured but why there was no action in the case for such a long time. When we got an FIR registered, Bhardwaj should have been charged under sections of attempt to murder,” she said.The 16-year-old, who attends a govt school, said the attack on her father left a traumatic impact on her and she was scared of going to school for a long time. “I was afraid that someone could be following me or I could be attacked. I kept delaying re-joining school till my parents convinced me that I would be safe,” she added.“I wanted to talk about things no one was paying attention to, like exam paper leaks and recruitment exam delays. I wanted to raise my voice against it. articles.title: A 33-year-old entrepreneur paid $2.55 million for a neglected 81-room Arkansas hotel; after moving into the property himself, he is spending another $1.1 million rebuilding it
articles.summary: US News: Some learn business, others are born with a hunch for it. When it comes to Greg Clark, it seems the latter holds true. At 19, he quit his job, paid hi.
articles.body: Some learn business, others are born with a hunch for it. When it comes to Greg Clark, it seems the latter holds true. At 19, he quit his job, paid his rent and was left with just $20 to his name. Today, he is renovating an 81-room hotel in Eureka Springs with a $1.1 million budget. The project, called Hotel Expedition, focuses on creating unique experiences with amenities like yoga and a fire pit, according to a report by PEOPLE.From side hustle to businessWhen Clark quit his job, he went back to live with his mom and began buying and selling used tyres on Craigslist out of her carport. This side hustle eventually grew into a multi-state, multi-location automotive business. However, in 2020, when the pandemic hit, Clark began looking for other avenues that could sustain his family without him having to devote 100-hour work weeks.“I found real estate and ended up falling in love with renovating old homes, but not so much with being a landlord,” the 33-year-old told the outlet. “I then turned to short-term rentals and really enjoyed the hospitality side of this business. I was finally able to combine creating beautiful spaces with the dopamine I get from other people loving these spaces.”This newfound love led to Clark moving from short-term rentals to larger hospitality projects. In late 2025, he bought his first hotel in Montana near Yellowstone National Park. After a complete renovation, it opened in early 2026. Despite the Montana hotel not being profitable, Clark says the experience solidified his passion for the business. “I was hooked for life now, so you could almost say these have turned into midlife crisis passion projects where I want to just push the boundaries of what guests accept as normal in hotels, and let my creativity explode on our canvases,” he said.A new projectNow, the entrepreneur is taking up his biggest project yet. An 81-room hotel in Eureka Springs, which he purchased for $2.55 million. He had budgeted another $1.1 million for renovations, including furniture, fixtures and equipment. He’s also living on-site while overseeing the massive renovation, which he hopes to complete in time for a grand opening around Christmas 2026.The Eureka Springs property was built in 1993 as a Holiday Inn Holidome, a style of hotel popular in the 1990s that centred guest rooms around an indoor pool area. According to Clark, the building was constructed by stacking concrete blocks in a pyramid-like structure, meaning each guest room is essentially a 25-by-12-foot concrete block that was craned into place.The project, which Clark has dubbed Hotel Expedition, is part of his larger goal to build a collection of 10 curated hotels over the next seven years. “I was inspired to buy this 81-room hotel the moment I walked the property and set foot inside the pool atrium,” Clark said, adding, “I knew right then and there, if I can just get everything else right with this property, this room will never go out of style.”He was drawn to Eureka Springs, which sits in the heart of the Ozarks, in part because of the growth of northwest Arkansas and the area’s attractions, including its historic landmarks, winding roads and rivers, as well as cave dining restaurants.However, transforming the property according to his vision is not proving to be an easy feat. Among the most pressing issues are a pool and hot tub that were in such a poor condition that they had to be closed to guests, along with a damaged elevator and multiple HVAC systems that need to be replaced. The HVAC work alone requires a special crane and large commercial package units.The lobby is also currently closed because guests cannot easily move through the space, making its completion one of Clark’s top priorities in the coming weeks. And as with any renovation of a building that has gone more than 30 years without proper care, Clark said the project has brought plenty of unexpected surprises.The property has also faced significant deferred maintenance, including issues involving its septic systems and roof. Those unexpected costs, along with HVAC expenses that have climbed into the hundreds of thousands of dollars, have forced Clark to make some difficult decisions about where to spend the renovation budget.A luxury escape without the price“We want to offer a level of amenities that cater to guests who want more out of their travel than just a bed and a warm shower,” he said. That vision includes a spa with an in-house masseuse, morning yoga, bracelet-making classes, movie nights by the pool and s’mores kits for guests to enjoy around the property’s fire pits. The goal is to make guests feel as though they’re staying at an upscale resort without the upscale price tag.Clark expects nightly rates to range from around $110 on a weekday to as much as $380 during an event weekend, depending on the season. In order to understand the hotel's target guest, he has also been travelling around the country and sometimes internationally to study hotels serving a similar audience.To keep things interesting, he is documenting the entire process on TikTok. Initially, he began sharing it to be able to look back on the progress and remember the transformation. But then, his videos went viral, amassing millions of views and hundreds of comments. “I had no idea millions of people would want to follow the journey,” he said. “The response has been very overwhelming and very mind-blowing.”“I hope followers can take away that I’m just an average dude; I’m not a corporation, a team of board members, or some rich trust fund kid,” he adds. “This goal is obtainable for any average, normal American.” One phrase in particular has become a personal mantra for him: “If they can do it, I can do it.”Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: 'Bound to breed contempt for law': SC judge Bhuyan on police action at Jantar Mantar protest
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Supreme Court judge Justice Ujjal Bhuyan criticised police officers over the alleged assault on protesting students during the NEET agitati.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Supreme Court judge Justice Ujjal Bhuyan criticised police officers over the alleged assault on protesting students during the NEET agitation at Jantar Mantar and said that the detachment expected of officials appears to be disappearing.While speaking at the launch of former secretary (security) Yashovardhan Azad's book "Policing the Republic", Justice Bhuyan said that police must maintain their credibility because people seek their help when they feel wronged."All of us are dismayed when we see young officers of the Indian Police Service personally going and assaulting protesters and demonstrators. This is something very, very distressing to observe. The detachment expected of police officers somehow seems to be disappearing, and this is indeed a matter of grave concern," Justice Bhuyan said."For most common people, a policeman on the street wearing a whistle and a lathi represents the power and authority of the state. When they feel wronged, they seek the help of the police. It is, therefore, of utmost importance that the police force maintains its credibility. It can do so only by strictly adhering to the Constitution, by functioning as a truly professional force, acting impartially, displaying courage and acting with conviction, maintaining integrity and adhering to secular principles, thereby upholding the rule of law," he said.The Supreme Court judge further said that if government functionaries become lawbreakers, it is bound to breed contempt for the law and encourage lawlessness."If the functionaries of the government become lawbreakers, it is bound to breed contempt for the law and will encourage lawlessness. No civilised nation can permit that to happen. Does a citizen shed his fundamental right the moment a policeman arrests him?" Justice Bhuyan said.The alleged use of force by Delhi Police during the July 20 student protests at Jantar Mantar and the march towards Parliament has come under the Supreme Court's scrutiny, with the court constituting a high-level panel to examine complaints of excessive force.The panel, headed by former Supreme Court judge Justice R Subhash Reddy, will investigate allegations against Delhi Police and examine evidence including CCTV footage and videos of the protests.Among the allegations to be examined are the use of lathis, tear gas, pellet guns and electronic batons, as well as claims of targeted harassment and molestation of women protesters.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Slow Horses writer Will Smith says Jersey helped shape career
articles.summary: Emmy Award winner Will Smith says the island was a creative and supportive environment growing up.
articles.body:
The lead writer behind hit television drama Slow Horses has credited Jersey with helping launch his career.

Three-time Emmy Award winner Will Smith, creator of the Apple TV+ spy drama which follows a team of failed or disgraced MI5 agents led by Jackson Lamb - played by Sir Gary Oldman, grew up on the island and attended Victoria College.

Smith said Jersey's creative community provided a "fertile, supportive environment" which helped lay the foundations for his success.

Slow Horses is up for nine awards at the upcoming Primetime Emmys in Los Angeles on 14 September, with Smith nominated in the Outstanding Writing For A Drama Series category.

"I wouldn't be doing it without Jersey and the people that I grew up with," Smith, who won the same category in 2024, said.

Smith, who is now based in London and previously won two Emmys for his work on political comedy show Veep, said he had the "fondest possible memories" of his childhood.

He said Jersey continued to inspire his work and praised the teachers who encouraged his love of storytelling.

Smith, whose acting credits include The Thick of It, Citizen Khan and Paddington, said the island "felt very safe" while he was growing up.

"It was a beautiful landscape - it was pretty idyllic really," he added.

Despite already winning international awards, Smith said attending television's biggest ceremonies still felt surreal.

"It's always amazing the company you're in with the nominations," he said.

"Last year, Harrison Ford was there and I can technically say I've been in the same room as Harrison Ford.

"If you'd told my seven-year-old self, who was a massive Star Wars and Indiana Jones fan, that one day I'd be sitting in an awards ceremony with him, it would have blown my mind."

Smith said winning an Emmy for Slow Horses was particularly meaningful because he had not expected to hear his name called.

"You can't control whether people love your show," he said.

"You've got to get into a state where if you write something and nobody reads it, you're still happy that you did it.

"If you can get into that zone, it's so much healthier because then you're always succeeding on your own terms."

articles.title: In 2024, Utah recycled 15,000 cubic yards of 30-year-old highway concrete on site; enough to fill two Goodyear Blimps became road base for new interchanges
articles.summary: US News: What if an old highway could become part of the new one? In Utah, that is exactly what happened. The Utah Department of Transportation (UDOT) recycled.
articles.body: What if an old highway could become part of the new one? In Utah, that is exactly what happened. The Utah Department of Transportation (UDOT) recycled around 15,000 cubic yards of concrete from the old Bangerter Highway in 2024, crushing it on site and reusing it as road base for new highway interchanges. The amount of concrete was roughly equivalent to the volume of two Goodyear Blimps, according to UDOT. Rather than sending the decades-old pavement away as construction waste, crews processed it where it was removed, reducing the number of truck journeys needed to transport the material.A 30-year-old highway gets a second lifeThe concrete came from sections of Bangerter Highway that had been in place for about three decades. As part of a major upgrade, crews needed to remove portions of the old roadway to make way for new freeway-style interchanges. Instead of treating the demolished pavement as waste, UDOT turned it into raw material for the replacement infrastructure.The recycling process took place over roughly five months. Heavy equipment first broke the existing concrete into manageable pieces. The material was then fed into a large crushing machine, where it was reduced to smaller fragments. A magnet inside the crusher separated the steel reinforcing bars, or rebar, from the concrete. The recovered metal was also recycled. The crushed concrete was subsequently processed into road base, the structural layer placed beneath pavement and other roadway surfaces. In effect, part of the old Bangerter Highway became the foundation for its replacement.Why recycle concrete on site?Construction projects can generate enormous quantities of material that must otherwise be hauled away. Moving that material requires repeated truck trips, adding transportation costs, traffic and fuel consumption.By crushing and reusing the concrete at the construction site, UDOT avoided transporting thousands of cubic yards of material elsewhere. The agency said the approach was intended in part to reduce truck trips around the project area.The project also demonstrates how demolished infrastructure can become a resource rather than simply entering the waste stream. Concrete and asphalt are among the major materials used in road construction that can be recovered and reused, although the exact recycling process depends on the material and project.The bigger Bangerter Highway transformationThe concrete recycling was part of a much larger effort to transform Bangerter Highway, a major north-south route through Salt Lake Valley. For more than a decade, UDOT has been working to replace traffic-signal-controlled intersections along the highway with freeway-style interchanges. In 2024, four interchanges were under construction at 13400 South, 9800 South, 4700 South and 2700 West. The overall programme was valued at about $415.3 million.Bangerter Highway carried roughly 60,000 vehicles a day, making the corridor particularly important to commuters and other travellers in the rapidly growing western part of the Salt Lake Valley. The interchange projects were designed to eliminate additional traffic lights, allowing vehicles to move through the corridor with fewer stops while improving the highway’s capacity and safety. And there was another unusual detail to the construction: some of the material being used to build that future highway had already spent decades serving the same road.From old pavement to new infrastructureThe idea is simple but striking: break down the old road, separate what can be recovered, process it and put it back into the new one. The 15,000 cubic yards of concrete recycled at the 4700 South project therefore did not simply disappear when the old pavement was demolished. Much of it was given another role, this time beneath the infrastructure being built to replace it. It is a small example of a larger shift in construction: sometimes, the material needed to build the next road is already sitting underneath the one being torn down.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: UN approves resolution to declare Nov 27 as ‘International Day For Elimination Of Child, Early & Forced Marriage’
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: In a significant development that brings focus on the need to step up action to deliver on the Sustainable Development Goals 2030, the Unit.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: In a significant development that brings focus on the need to step up action to deliver on the Sustainable Development Goals 2030, the United Nations (UN) has declared November 27 the International Day for the Elimination of Child, Early and Forced Marriage. The date carries special significance for India, which backed the resolution steered by Sierra Leone, as it was on Nov 27 that the govt had launched the ‘Bal Vivah Mukt Bharat’ campaign in 2024.Even though underage marriage has been declining over the decades, the numbers are still a concern calling for greater efforts to eradicate the problem. According to the 2019-21 National Family Health Survey (NFHS-5), 23.3% of women aged 20-24 were married before the age of 18. This came down to 20.1% in NFHS-6 (2023-24).Just Rights for Children founder Bhuwan Ribhu, who has been vociferously advocating for a dedicated day and has worked closely with the drafting of the resolution, said that the announcement is very significant for India as it is an opportunity to lead by example and meet the elimination targets.Welcoming the UN approval for the demand from countries across the world, Ribhu said, “Today marks the tipping point, showing that the end of the crime of child marriage is inevitable and imminent. Now is the time for governments globally to provide decisive leadership to end child marriage by 2030 and ensure education, protection and development of every child to realise their full potential. I am grateful to the First Lady of Sierra Leone for her leadership in championing this cause and would also like to thank the countries that co-sponsored our resolution. “ He was present at the UN as the civil society representative when the UN approved the resolution.“The Government of India has set a target of reducing the prevalence of child marriage by 10% by 2026. With continued efforts at the national and state levels, the prevalence of child marriage in India is expected to fall below 15% by the end of 2026. The global commitment to eliminate child marriage by 2030 is aligned with target 5.3 of Sustainable Development Goal 5 (Gender Equality), which calls for the elimination of all harmful practices, including child, early, and forced marriage,” Ribhu added.He shared that plans are afoot to hold extensive outreach campaigns in coordination with the govt and states ahead of November 27 to ensure that the day becomes a space to dwell on progress made and the way forward and does not end up as a symbolic reminder of the problem.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: True Samaritans: Indian volunteers take up grim task of cleaning decomposed bodies in Kathmandu
articles.summary: South Asia News: DEHRADUN: As rescue agencies continue recovering bodies from flash flood-hit areas in Nepal and bringing them to Kathmandu mortuaries, a group of youn.
articles.body: DEHRADUN: As rescue agencies continue recovering bodies from flash flood-hit areas in Nepal and bringing them to Kathmandu mortuaries, a group of young Indian volunteers has taken up a task few are willing to do — cleaning decomposed bodies before they are handed over to families and authorities for the last rites. The group has helped clean more than 30 bodies till now.At least seven volunteers -- Harteerath Singh, Neha Singh, Jag Singh, Jaskaran Singh, Ravi Singh, Amitose Singh and Harry Singh -- of Hemkunt Foundation, a Gurgaon-based non-profit organisation, are carrying out the work at the morgue of Maharajgunj Medical Campus, Kathmandu.One of the volunteers, Neha Singh, told TOI Friday that she travelled from Mumbai to Kathmandu for the voluntary service after coming across a social media post by the foundation, requesting volunteers to join them in Nepal. “The next thing I did was to fly down to Kathmandu without expecting anything,” she said, adding that volunteers were not known to each other before reaching there; and were now working as a family in this ‘sewa’ (selfless service).They say that they are totally focused on the task, and even the terrible stench of bodies has failed to deter them. Neha said, “We are here for the respect of the departed souls and the bereaved families. We don’t seek any publicity in that.”Another member of the group, Harteerath Singh, elaborated on some of the challenges being faced by them. “Due to the acute stench, sometimes, it becomes unbearable for us to stand inside the morgue even for a minute,” he pointed out.“But this is the ultimate ‘sewa’. At times, we don’t even bother to wear masks or gloves. We cover our faces with one corner of the turban cloth and just go inside to clean the bodies and floors of the morgue -- something which even the local authorities may not be willing to do,” Singh said.“We also see the positive side of it. It is the biggest opportunity for us to serve humanity.”Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Plea to give Thames seals space for everyone's safety
articles.summary: Getting too close to the animals spotted along the River Thames can be harmful for both them and members of the public, a charity says.
articles.body:
Marmalade the harbour seal was a familiar visitor to the River Thames, often popping up at Greenwich and Rotherhithe in south-east London.

She was given her nickname because of her bright golden-coloured coat.

However, as the number of seal sightings along the river increases, charity Thames Seal Watch has urged members of the public to give the animals space.

Despite looking cute, Emma Kelly from the charity says: "They can bite and they carry zoonotic diseases which are not very pleasant if you were to suffer a bite.

"They will do that to protect themselves."

She says getting close to the animals can cause them distress and stress, which could lead to their death.

The charity says more and more of the seals are travelling further up the river, with one spotted as far west as Windsor.

It is thought there are about 3,500 seals living in the Thames and that they mostly stay around the estuary, east of London.

Marmalade was considered rare because there are only 500 harbour seals living in the river, compared with about 3,000 of the more common grey seals.

Gareth Richards from UK Seal Alliance says "seals are very transient, and will basically go to where there is good fish stocks".

He says "seals can swim from anything between 60 and 80 miles a day".

Because they are being spotted more frequently, Richards says he would like to see further protection of the animals in law.

Neither grey nor harbour seals are protected from intentional or reckless disturbance under the Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981.

In May, UK Seal Alliance launched its Give Seals Space campaign, calling on the government to reconsider previous recommendations and provide the two species "with the legal protection they deserve".

The campaign warns that they are highly sensitive to disturbance from the public, animals and drones.

It states these can have long-lasting consequences to the animals' health and that it can lead to pup abandonment, wasted energy from staying alert and injuries from panic fleeing.

The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) says: "We have a suite of legislative protections in place which make it an offence to take, injure, capture or kill a seal."

As for Marmalade, she contracted a parasite disease and died in May.

Some volunteers from Thames Seal Watch, including Kelly, gathered at one of her favourite spots near the University of Greenwich for a short memorial.

Flowers were thrown into the river and a small plaque in her memory was erected.

Kelly says: "Marmalade was really special to the community.

"We created a community around Marmalade where there was lots of us to keep an eye on her and ensure she stayed safe."

Marmalade also helped attract a number of new volunteers to the charity, and all those at the memorial made a commitment that they would continue to help London's wildlife in the best way they can.

articles.summary: US News: US government investigators subjected roughly 50 members of the Joint Staff to polygraph tests over leaks to journalists. The investigation centred on.
articles.body: US government investigators subjected roughly 50 members of the Joint Staff to polygraph tests over leaks to journalists. The investigation centred on leaks about dwindling US stocks of advanced weapons, according to reports.According to multiple media reports, members of the Joint Staff were tested in August after media reports detailed shortages of crucial munitions, including long-range missiles and Patriot interceptors, the Times reported, citing officials briefed on the move.The tests sought to determine whether military officers and civilian employees had disclosed classified information to journalists, including details about diminished US munitions stocks.CBS News reported that several dozen people had also been tested earlier in the summer, including officials at US Central Command and other combatant commands.Polygraphs are routinely used every few years to recertify security clearances for officials with access to top-secret information or special access programmes. However, officials told CBS News that the number of people tested in this case was highly unusual.The New York Times reported that the US Joint Staff has between 1,500 and 2,000 officers and officials, coordinating operations, policy and war plans with combatant commanders around the world.Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell, meanwhile, said the department “does not comment on internal personnel or investigative matters but takes all leaks of classified national security information extremely seriously and investigates accordingly.”The questions reportedly covered a range of national security matters. Sources quoted by CBS News said that no one failed the questions specifically aimed at determining whether they had leaked information to the media.President Donald Trump was furious about the leaks, according to three CBS News sources who spoke on condition of anonymity. One source said only a very small group of people had access to the classified weapons information, raising concerns over whether anyone could be acting as a foreign intelligence asset.Not all senior officials were tested. A senior Pentagon official told CBS News that chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Gen. Dan Caine was not subjected to a polygraph.The scope of the testing comes after defence secretary Pete Hegseth announced in July that the Pentagon and Justice Department had formed a joint task force to identify and prosecute suspected leakers. “When a leak of department information occurs today, it's critical that we provide the Department of Justice and other partners in federal law enforcement — including the FBI — with actionable information as quickly as possible,” Hegseth said. “Leaked information risks lives.”The FBI was not involved in the latest round of polygraph tests, with the US military conducting the investigation itself.Federal law and Pentagon regulations place restrictions on the use of polygraphs and require procedural safeguards, including consent in certain investigative circumstancesCatch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Oscar-winning actor Paul Newman gave 7.5 Connecticut acres to Westport in 1997; after his death, it helped form a 38-acre preserve with land bought for $3.75 million
articles.summary: US News: Explore the story behind Paul Newman's generous donation of land to create the Newman/Poses Nature Preserve, a natural retreat that supports wildlife and offers recreational opportunities in Westport, Connecticut.
articles.body: Hollywood stars have often left behind buildings, awards and film memorabilia, but Paul Newman left something quieter: a piece of woodland in his adopted hometown of Westport, Connecticut. In 1997, the Oscar-winning actor donated 7.5 acres beside his home to the town, helping protect a larger area of open space that later became the Newman/Poses Nature Preserve. Following Newman’s death in 2008, his family supported naming the preserve in his honour, transforming land once connected to his private life into a public natural retreat.According to the Connecticut Post, the Newman/Poses Nature Preserve is a roughly 38-acre tract at the corner of Bayberry Lane, Coleytown Road and Easton Road in Westport. In 1997, Paul Newman donated 7.5 acres to the town, while another 29.9 acres were acquired from the Poses family for $3.75 million. The property includes woods, a meadow, wetlands and the Aspetuck River, and is maintained as open space by the Aspetuck Land Trust.A gift rooted in Newman's own lifeNewman's connection to the property was personal. He and his wife, actress Joanne Woodward, had made Westport their home, and their children grew up exploring the land around the family property. Lissy Newman later recalled walking through the woods with her father and talking with him there. For the Newman family, preserving the land was less about creating a memorial than about protecting a place full of memories.The actor had also developed a reputation for supporting conservation in his community and was a longtime supporter of the Aspetuck Land Trust, which would eventually help maintain the preserve. After Newman’s death in September 2008, his daughters Lissy and Clea worked with the land trust and town officials to turn the already protected property into a formally designated nature preserve. Although Newman had generally been reluctant to have public places named after him, his family made an exception for the woodland because of his personal connection to the land and his enjoyment of walking there. In 2010, Westport’s Representative Town Meeting unanimously approved the name Newman/Poses Nature Preserve, honouring both Newman and the Poses family, whose land had also become part of the preserve.Where woodland meets riverThe preserve is more than a patch of trees. Its ecological value comes partly from the mixture of habitats packed into a relatively small area. The site includes woodland, meadow, wetlands, streams and the Aspetuck River. Trails wind through these different environments, while some wetland crossings use raised boardwalks to reduce disturbance. The town has kept the area for passive recreation, allowing activities such as walking and, in permitted areas, fishing, while prohibiting development.The preserve's mix of woodland and open habitat supports a range of wildlife. Contemporary reporting on the site described birds, chipmunks, squirrels and coyotes, while state wildlife officials noted that its combination of native grasses, wetlands, streams and meadow provided habitat useful for feeding, nesting and seasonal activity. The area also supports turtles, including the North American wood turtle and eastern box turtle, which can use open-canopy upland areas for summer foraging.Research published in Ecosphere has more recently reinforced the importance of protecting Connecticut's forest habitat. Examining bird communities across the state, researchers found that increasing forest fragmentation was associated with declines in community density, while habitat characteristics influenced species richness. The findings underline how retaining sizeable, functioning habitat can be important for birds living in an increasingly developed landscape.A memorial that became public landIn 2011, the Newman/Poses Nature Preserve was accessible to the public. Visitors were taken on a tour of the trails that passed through woods and meadow and even along the Aspetuck River. The property was owned by the town and managed by the Aspetuck Land Trust, turning land once used mainly by neighbours into a public space. Newman's life history makes the narrative especially relevant. Newman was known for Hollywood glamour, but he also spent his later years on philanthropy and auto racing, and remained deeply devoted to the places he called home.What began in 1997 as a 7.5-acre donation eventually became part of a much larger protected area. The $3.75-million purchase of the neighbouring Poses property expanded the preserve, while Newman’s death in 2008 brought renewed attention to his connection with the land. In 2010, the community named the protected area the Newman/Poses Nature Preserve. Today, the preserve encompasses nearly 38 acres of woodland, meadow and river habitat, preserving a piece of Newman’s legacy for both people and wildlife.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In the 1920s, radio star Will Rogers built a 186-acre Pacific Palisades ranch; after his widow died in 1944, the property became a California state historic park
articles.summary: US News: The Will Rogers State Historic Park in Pacific Palisades, established in honor of the famed radio star and actor, faced irreparable damage after a fire destroyed the iconic Ranch House. Opened to the public after restoration, the park continues to honor Rogers' legacy while offering hiking and outdoor activities.
articles.body: Will Rogers started acquiring property in the hills above Santa Monica in the early 1920s, assembling a private 186-acre ranch overlooking the Pacific Ocean in what is now Pacific Palisades; the land would not become a state park until 1944. California State Parks and other secondary sources both describe the property as 186 acres. In the early 1930s, Will Rogers was among the highest-paid actors in Hollywood, and the ranch gave him a place to ride horses and play polo.The 31-room Ranch House, built in 1926The centerpiece of the property was a 31-room ranch house, according to California State Parks, where Rogers and his wife, Betty, raised their three children: Will Jr., Mary, and Jim. The National Register of Historic Places lists the house's year of construction as 1926, with a period of significance spanning 1925 to 1949, reflecting the fuller span of Rogers' activity on the land rather than the building alone. That same federal listing records the house's original address as 14253 Sunset Boulevard, the address on file when it joined the Register in 1971; the park's current address is 1501 Will Rogers State Park Road.Rogers dies in a plane crash with Wiley PostHowever, Rogers' career ended on August 15, 1935, when he died in a plane crash with fellow aviator Wiley Post in Alaska. Betty Rogers took possession of the property and continued hosting polo games at the ranch field. She died in 1944, the same year she ensured the 186-acre property would pass into public hands: California State Parks says she wanted the ranch preserved as a memorial to her husband, and the land became Will Rogers State Historic Park, open to the public ever since. The ranch house was listed in the National Register of Historic Places on February 24, 1971.January 2025: The Palisades fire destroys the Ranch HouseThe Palisades Fire ravaged the ranch house in Will Rogers State Historic Park in January 2025. As ICT News explains, the fire completely destroyed the house in the Los Angeles fires of Jan. 8. However, state parks personnel saved several pieces of artwork and personal belongings before the flames engulfed the structure. Jennifer Rogers-Etcheverry, a great-granddaughter of Rogers, indicated that she wanted to get involved in the park's restoration efforts. The park was owned by California State Parks the entire time, but the park itself was closed due to fire, including popular trails like those leading to Inspiration Point, while the damage was being assessed. The regulation-sized polo field within the park, which had hosted polo matches on the very ground Rogers rode across, escaped relatively unscathed from the fire.The park reopens after a ten-month closure The park had been closed for ten months to conduct clean-up and assess the extent of damage. According to California State Parks and various other news sources like LAist and OutdoorHub, the park opened its doors to the public again on November 8, 2025, with operating hours set to run from 8 a.m. until sunset, and with limited on-site parking. As per CBS LA, all nine miles of trails in the park were open to the public on that day except the Backbone Trail, the Rivas Canyon and Temescal Trail, and portions of the Inspiration Point Trailhead. Opening day featured guided hikes, historical walks, a polo demonstration, free coffee and ice cream, and lawn games, giving residents their first chance in nearly a year to walk the grounds Rogers once called home.The 31-room ranch house burned down entirely in the fire, leaving nothing except its foundation, while a security fence has been erected around the remains, which comprise two chimneys and portions of the original stonework walks. According to California State Parks, the future of this site would depend on a public outreach program to start in 2026, which would help restore the Will Rogers State Historic Park as a homage to his former ranch residence.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: 'Built to confuse spirits': Inside California's Winchester Mystery House, 104 after owner's death
articles.summary: News News: More than a century after American philanthropist Sarah Winchester died, the sprawling mansion she spent nearly four decades building continues to sta.
articles.body: More than a century after American philanthropist Sarah Winchester died, the sprawling mansion she spent nearly four decades building continues to stand as one of America's most unusual properties and often belived to be 'haunted'.Winchester Mystery House in San Jose, California, was once the private residence of Winchester heiress Sarah Lockwood Pardee Winchester. She died exactly 104 years ago on September 5, 1922, bringing an end to the construction that had transformed an eight-room farmhouse into a sprawling architectural labyrinth.The story behind the unusual construction is rooted in tragedy. Winchester lost her infant daughter to illness and, a few years later, her husband, William Wirt Winchester, to tuberculosis. Following her husband’s death, she left their home in New Haven, Connecticut, and moved to San Jose.According to popular legend, Winchester consulted a medium who told her that the spirits of people killed by Winchester rifles were seeking revenge. She was supposedly advised to move west and keep building a house continuously to confuse the spirits.There is no conclusive evidence that this was the reason for the construction. But the story, combined with the mansion’s bizarre design, has fuelled its reputation as a haunted house for more than a century.Construction continued from 1886 until Winchester’s death in 1922, with the property expanding into an architectural labyrinth. The mansion eventually contained 10,000 windows, 2,000 doors, 52 skylights, 47 stairways and fireplaces, 17 chimneys, 13 bathrooms and six kitchens.Among its most famous features are staircases that abruptly end at ceilings, doors that open onto walls and windows positioned in unusual locations; details that have helped keep the mystery surrounding the property alive.The house was reportedly built at a cost of about $5 million by 1923, equivalent to roughly $71 million today.The 1906 San Francisco earthquake also damaged parts of the mansion and altered sections of its upper levels.Winchester’s death brought the extraordinary construction project to an end. Less than a year later, on June 30, 1923, the property opened to the public.Today, the Winchester Mystery House is a historic landmark and tourist attraction that draws visitors with a combination of architectural eccentricity, history and its enduring ghost story.More than 100 years after Winchester stopped building, the question of why she created such an unusual home remains part of the property's enduring appeal.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision?
