articles.title: In 1891, Red Cross founder Clara Barton received part of an 80-acre Maryland gift; today her home anchors a 22-acre National Park Service landscape
articles.summary: US News: Explore the legacy of Clara Barton, founder of the Red Cross, at her historic home in Glen Echo, Maryland, now part of a 22-acre National Park. Learn about the house's transformation from a relief warehouse to her residence and its journey to becoming a National Historic Site.
articles.body: In the late nineteenth century, the Baltzley brothers in Maryland bought land alongside the Potomac River, hoping to turn the area into a cultural retreat in the style of the Chautauqua movement. But to make their unproven venture look respectable, the brothers needed a name that people were already familiar with. So they turned to Clara Barton, the founder of the American Red Cross, and gave her part of the land they had acquired.The gift that built a homeThe Baltzleys called the land the National Chautauqua of Glen Echo, and Barton later built her home there. According to a landscape history published by the National Park Service, the 22 acre cultural landscape that survives today sits in Montgomery County and combines two separate National Park Service units, Glen Echo Park and the Clara Barton National Historic Site. The property includes part of the 80 acres that Edward and Edwin Baltzley donated in 1891 to establish the Chautauqua, and they gifted a portion of that land to Barton, the founder of the American Red Cross, while also supplying the labour and materials used to build her house. The same history traces how the site shifted from an educational campus into an amusement park once the Chautauqua idea struggled to take hold, with Edwin Baltzley renting the grounds out to vaudeville acts and the first amusement park structures going up by 1899. Barton needed a base from which to run relief operations, and the house built for her was no ordinary cottage. It grew to thirty rooms across several floors, with enough space built in to double as storage and office space whenever disaster relief work demanded it.From warehouse to residenceBarton's relationship with the house was not as simple as moving in and staying put. She lived there briefly in 1891, not long after it was completed, then left for several years before returning in 1897 once the trolley line reached Glen Echo and made the location far easier to reach day to day. During that gap, the house served as an American Red Cross warehouse, storing supplies and equipment the organisation needed for the floods, fires and other disasters it responded to. Once Barton moved back in for good, the house also became the Red Cross's national headquarters, a role it held from 1897 until 1904. She spent the final fifteen years of her life running the organisation from those same rooms, which had once held nothing but crates of relief supplies.Guides who lead tours through the property still point out small details that reveal her frugal habits, and the National Park Service notes that some of the interior walls and ceilings are covered in muslin, the same material used in field bandages, rather than plaster. The house also carried the Red Cross emblem worked into its stained glass windows, a detail that quietly tied her home to the organisation she had spent decades building.A landscape preserved decades laterThe historical recognition of the property’s value took too long to arrive. Barton’s house passed into private hands after her death and stayed that way for roughly fifty years before a group called Friends of Clara Barton bought it in the 1960s specifically to preserve it. A marker placed at the site, recorded by the Historical Marker Database, notes that the house was built in 1891 by Edward and Edwin Baltzley as part of the National Chautauqua at Glen Echo and that it later became a National Historic Site under the National Park Service. Congress declared the house a National Historic Landmark in January 1965, and legislation passed in 1974 established it as the Clara Barton National Historic Site, the first such site in the country dedicated to the achievements of a woman. The National Park Service formally acquired the property the following year, in April 1975, through a donation from the Friends of Clara Barton.What fascinates the visitors and what they encounter now extends well beyond the house alone. Barton’s home sits within a broader stretch of land estimated at 22 acres in total. The National Park Service manages together with the adjoining Glen Echo Park, a former amusement park that operated on neighbouring ground until the late 1960s. The two properties share a cultural landscape designation, linking Barton’s story to the wider history of the land. More than a century later, it is Barton’s story, not theirs, that draws people to Glen Echo.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: In 2016, Florida’s New Smyrna Beach used living shorelines during Hurricane Matthew; the structures stayed intact despite 90 mph winds
articles.summary: US News: When Hurricane Matthew struck Florida in October 2016, New Smyrna Beach faced winds of more than 90 miles per hour and water levels around four feet a.
articles.body: When Hurricane Matthew struck Florida in October 2016, New Smyrna Beach faced winds of more than 90 miles per hour and water levels around four feet above normal. Along the coast, those conditions put shoreline protection to a serious test. But one demonstration site emerged with an unexpected result. A living shoreline project supported by NOAA and the St Johns River Water Management District remained largely intact after the storm, with minimal erosion. Instead of depending on conventional seawalls or bulkheads, the project used vegetation, sand and limited amounts of rock to stabilise the shoreline while also providing habitat for wildlife. The demonstration area was directly in the path of Matthew's most destructive winds, making its survival particularly notable. Nearby, a building even lost its roof during the storm. Yet the living shoreline structures held firm. The experience offered a striking example of how natural shoreline protection could withstand powerful hurricane conditions.How do living shorelines protect coasts during stormsLiving shorelines take a different approach from traditional coastal defences. Rather than relying entirely on concrete, bulkheads or seawalls, they incorporate natural materials such as vegetation, sand and limited amounts of rock. According to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, these materials help shorelines withstand the energy carried by storm surges and waves while also creating habitat for fish and wildlife. The approach is intended to reduce erosion while strengthening the resilience of coastal areas.That distinction became important when Hurricane Matthew arrived. Conventional hardened structures can sometimes increase coastal erosion and provide little habitat. Living shorelines, by contrast, combine coastal protection with ecological benefits. The New Smyrna Beach project therefore served not only as a demonstration of different shoreline techniques, but also as an opportunity to see how those approaches performed when confronted with an actual hurricane.How did Hurricane Matthew test the living shorelineThe conditions around New Smyrna Beach were severe enough to expose weaknesses in coastal structures. Winds exceeded 90 miles per hour, a nearby building lost its roof, and water levels rose roughly four feet above normal. The demonstration shoreline also faced north, directly towards the direction from which the most destructive winds arrived. Yet when the storm had passed, NOAA found that the structures were still standing and had suffered minimal erosion.The result was striking because the project was not tested under mild conditions. It faced a major hurricane with strong winds, elevated water and wave energy, making the outcome a useful demonstration of how natural shoreline techniques could perform during a storm. NOAA's assessment was direct: "after the hurricane, all structures in the area were intact, with minimal erosion."Living shorelines showed less damage after Hurricane MatthewEvidence from elsewhere along the coast provided another point of comparison. In the aftermath of Hurricane Matthew, the North Carolina Coastal Federation surveyed shorelines and found no visible damage at the living shorelines it examined. By comparison, at least half of the hardened shorelines in its survey had been damaged, including areas where sediment had been scoured from the front of structures or water had flowed over them, weakening them.The New Smyrna Beach experience therefore became part of a wider picture of how coastal communities might respond to storms. Living shorelines are not simply planted areas beside the water. They are a form of shoreline stabilisation designed to reduce erosion while also supporting habitat and coastal resilience. Hurricane Matthew provided an unusually demanding test, and the New Smyrna Beach demonstration structures emerged from it still standing, with little erosion.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Cornish charity backs push for legal protection of resting seals
articles.summary: The Seal Research Trust backs calls to make deliberate seal disturbance an offence.
articles.body:
A charity is backing a campaign calling for stronger legal protection for seals, saying human disturbance is harming their health and welfare.

The Seal Research Trust , based in Cornwall, has backed calls from the UK Seal Alliance to make the deliberate disturbance of seals an offence under the Wildlife and Countryside Act .

Trust founder Sue Sayers said seals resting on beaches were regularly being disturbed by people, causing stress, injury and sleep deprivation.

The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) said: "We have a suite of legislative protections in place which make it an offence to take, injure, capture or kill a seal."

Sayers said: "Seals need sleep just like we do... When they're disturbed, they can panic, stampede across a beach or throw themselves into the sea, risking serious injury."

The campaign follows concerns over what the trust described as the "hidden cost" of disturbance.

The charity said frequent interruptions could affect seals' immune systems, hormone levels and ability to recover between feeding trips.

Sayers also expressed concern about this year's seal pup season, describing it as one of the worst on record.

"More than half of the seal pups we've recorded so far this year have been dead or dying."

She said until this year, the trust had never recorded seal pups being born in every month of a calendar year, and believed climate change had influenced breeding patterns.

The Seal Research Trust advises anyone who encounteres a seal to stay at least 100m (328ft) away, avoid sharing its location on social media and never attempt to feed or move the animal.

In May, UK Seal Alliance launched its Give Seals Space , campaign, calling on the government to reconsider previous recommendations and provide the two species "with the legal protection they deserve".

The campaign warns that they are highly sensitive to disturbance from the public, animals and drones.

It states these can have long-lasting consequences to the animals' health and that it can lead to pup abandonment, wasted energy from staying alert and injuries from panic fleeing.

articles.title: Beavers released on Exmoor filmed showing signs of bonding
articles.summary: Conservationists say the budding relationship is "exciting" for the species and their habitat.
articles.body:
Conservationists are hopeful that two bonding beavers who were released into the wild earlier in 2026 could help to strengthen the population of the creatures.

The beavers, which live on the Holnicote Estate, Exmoor, Somerset, were captured on trail cameras grooming each other.

The semi-aquatic rodents were released in February as part of the National Trust's work to restore rivers, wetlands and floodplains on the 5,000-hectare site.

National Trust ranger Mathieu Burtschell said: "The fact that they have paired up is a good indication that they have found the right conditions at Holnicote, with enough suitable habitat, food and space to establish a territory together."

Beavers usually live in small family groups centred around an adult pair who then typically mate for life.

Once the creatures establish their territory, their dams, canals and wetlands can help to create new habitats for other wildlife and keep water in the landscape for longer.

Burtschell said the charity was hopeful the animals would explore, establish territories and start to form the relationships that were "so important" to a healthy beaver population.

"Seeing these two beavers together on the trail camera is really exciting.

"They are largely active at night, so trail cameras give us a valuable window into what they are doing when we are not there.

"If the pair remains together, they could eventually establish their own family group and help strengthen the beaver population across the estate," he added.

The beavers are being monitored by rangers to understand how they settle, move through the catchment and shape the surrounding habitat.

They were among two groups that were released freely in Somerset for the first time, following a decision from the government to approve the reintroduction of the animals in England in 2025.

The species had previously been reintroduced to the Holnicote Estate, but within closures.

articles.title: In 2017, New York high-school students were asked to redesign a downtown park; 9 years later, one of their winning ideas has finally been built in a $1 million project
articles.summary: US News: What began as a classroom design exercise by high-school students in New York has taken nearly a decade to become a reality. In 2017, students from No.
articles.body: What began as a classroom design exercise by high-school students in New York has taken nearly a decade to become a reality. In 2017, students from North Tonawanda High School's engineering academy were asked to imagine how a downtown park could be transformed. One of the winning ideas featured a clock tower and a landscaped gathering space.Nine years later, that concept has become part of a $1 million downtown improvement project in North Tonawanda, New York. The city recently marked the completion of Smart Growth 2.0, a redevelopment initiative that includes a new clock tower at Charles Fleischmann Park, upgraded walkways, landscaping, seating, lighting and other pedestrian improvements.The project was officially celebrated with a ribbon-cutting ceremony on September 2, 2026, bringing to life an idea that originated with local teenagers nearly a decade earlier.A student idea takes shapeThe clock tower is among the most visible changes at Charles Fleischmann Park. The concept traces back to 2017, when students were invited to think about what could make the small downtown park more attractive and useful to the community.The city eventually incorporated one of the students' winning concepts into Smart Growth 2.0. According to project documents, the park improvements include new landscaping, reconfigured walkways, benches, dining tables, bike racks, lighting and irrigation, along with a decorative clock feature.The new project also extends beyond the park. Webster Street received pedestrian lighting and improvements to deteriorated paving, while landscaping and placemaking elements were added around the downtown area. Electric vehicle charging stations were also installed at the Manhattan Street parking lot.Building on a decade-old investmentSmart Growth 2.0 is an extension of an earlier revitalisation programme that began in 2017. That year, North Tonawanda was selected for up to $2.5 million through New York's Western New York Smart Growth Community Fund, part of Buffalo Billion II. The earlier funding supported projects including 400 linear feet of new docks and utilities at Gateway Harbour, a new harbormaster facility, an expansion of Charles Fleischmann Park and pedestrian improvements across downtown. The city said the $2.5 million investment helped leverage another $5 million for related projects.The latest $1 million initiative was designed to build on those improvements by making downtown spaces more attractive, walkable and welcoming.Part of a $10-million downtown revivalSmart Growth 2.0 is one of 14 projects selected under North Tonawanda's $10 million Downtown Revitalisation Initiative award. The broader programme aims to strengthen the city's downtown and waterfront while encouraging new housing, business activity and public spaces.City officials say the improvements are intended to create a stronger identity for the downtown area. Mayor Austin Tylec described the project as a significant investment and an anchor for the city centre.Benjamin Bidell, a revitalisation specialist with the New York State Department of State, said the project was completed ahead of schedule and represents roughly the midway point of North Tonawanda's broader Downtown Revitalisation Initiative programme.From classroom sketches to a city landmarkThe transformation of the park is particularly notable because the idea did not begin with architects, developers or city planners. It started with students being asked to imagine what their own downtown could look like. Nearly a decade later, one of those ideas has moved from a school exercise into the physical landscape of the city.For North Tonawanda, the project is part of a much larger effort to revive its downtown. For the students who participated in the original design challenge, however, the new clock tower offers something more personal: a visible reminder that ideas developed in a classroom can sometimes take years, public investment and persistence to become reality.The completed project also reflects the city's broader shift toward pedestrian-friendly public spaces, combining landscaping, seating, lighting and other amenities designed to encourage people to spend more time downtown.As North Tonawanda continues implementing its Downtown Revitalisation Initiative projects, the student-inspired clock tower now stands as one of the clearest symbols of that transformation, connecting an idea imagined by teenagers in 2017 with a finished public space in 2026.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Russia hit Ukraine airports ahead of US envoys' visit in overnight strikes, Zelenskyy says
articles.summary: Europe News: Russia launched overnight strikes on airports in Kyiv and Boryspil ahead of a planned visit by US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, Ukrainian Pr.
articles.body: Russia launched overnight strikes on airports in Kyiv and Boryspil ahead of a planned visit by US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Saturday. Sharing the visuals of the aftermath, he linked the attacks to preparations for the American delegation’s possible arrival by aircraft.“There were also demonstrative Russian strikes on our airports overnight – in Kyiv and Boryspil. Deliberate, for the first time in a while,” Zelenskyy said in a post on X.“Clearly, these Russian strikes on the airports are a reaction to the discussions and preparations for the possibility of the U.S. side using an aircraft to travel to Ukraine and land at Kyiv Airport or Boryspil Airport,” he added.The planned visit by Witkoff and Kushner, who is US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law, is aimed at reviving peace talks amid an escalation in aerial attacks between Russia and Ukraine.Zelenskyy had on Friday said Kyiv would halt air attacks during the US envoys’ visit and urged Moscow to do the same.“Just as we did during previous diplomatic visits by the American side, we will ensure the normal functioning of Russian airspace so that the negotiators can arrive safely,” Zelenskyy said in a social media post. “There will be no airstrikes from our side, and Russia must do the same, ensuring there are no airstrikes from its side for the time needed to hold these talks and handle the logistical matters related to this American visit.”The latest Russian strikes killed four people and wounded five at a civilian industrial facility in Kamianske in Ukraine’s Dnipropetrovsk region, local officials said. Residential buildings were also damaged in several regions, including Kherson, Boryspil and Kharkiv.In Sumy and Mykolaiv, Russian drones struck shopping malls. Ukraine’s state emergency services said a 72-year-old man and a 17-year-old girl were wounded in the Mykolaiv attack.Russia’s defence ministry said its forces had struck two metallurgical plants in the Dnipropetrovsk region, describing them as major suppliers of metal products for Ukraine’s military production.Ukraine’s air force said Russia launched ballistic missiles from its Rostov and Voronezh regions and deployed 167 attack drones overnight. The drones included Shahed-type aircraft, around half of them jet-powered, along with Geran and decoy drones. Ukrainian air defences shot down or suppressed 128 drones, according to the Air Force.The air war has intensified as Russian and Ukrainian forces struggle to make significant progress along the roughly 1,250-kilometre front line.Zelenskyy said Kyiv had taken note of the airport strikes and warned that Ukraine would adjust its operations in Russian airspace.“Russian-Iranian ‘shaheds’ in response to American diplomacy. We have taken note of this Russian move, and next week we will adjust our operation accordingly regarding Russian airspace, which has become dangerous because of our drones and missiles in the sky,” he said.“Of course, there are and will be no threats to diplomacy from our side. Ukraine is interested in bringing peace closer. Russia will be held accountable for what it does,” he added.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Russian Assault On Hannivka Shows New Tactics Against Ukrainian Drones
articles.summary: Russia's attack on Hannivka showed emerging tactics that exploited gaps in Ukraine’s drone defenses using poor weather, small assault teams, and FPV drone in...
articles.body:
In late August, the Kremlin reiterated its pre-war objective of capturing the entirety of Donetsk Oblast by the end of the year. However, this goal will be difficult to achieve as Ukraine's drone-based defenses have effectively stalled the Russian offensive. In an effort to break this stalemate, Russia has introduced a number of new tactics on the battlefield, although none have produced significant gains. An emerging set of tactics was reportedly used during the recent Russian assault on Hannivka (Russian: Annovka), a town in Donetsk Oblast. A video posted by the Russian Ministry of Defense features a Russian drone operator describing the assault and reported capture of the town. His account provides insight into the latest tactics Russian forces are employing to overcome Ukrainian defenses and regain momentum.

The primary challenge facing the Russian offensive is Ukraine's extensive use of tactical drones. Ukrainian forces operate a diverse fleet that ranges from small reconnaissance and FPV strike drones to larger multirotor bombers, commonly referred to as Baba Yagas. These drones provide Ukrainian forces with persistent surveillance and strike capabilities across the front. They are operated by small teams dispersed throughout the region, often from concealed, protected locations. This dispersion, combined with the large number of drone teams, has made it difficult for Russian forces to locate and target them.

The growing range and capabilities of these drones have created extensive "kill zones" along the front . Within these areas, Ukrainian drones continuously patrol for Russian soldiers and vehicles, making movement extremely dangerous. These kill zones can extend 10 to 15 kilometers from the front, with some Ukrainian drone units striking targets at ranges of 20 to 30 kilometers. As drone technology improves, these zones are becoming deeper. As such, Russian forces must cross several kilometers of terrain under persistent drone surveillance before they can even reach Ukrainian defensive positions.

These kill zones inherently make it difficult for Russian forces to achieve the mass needed for an assault. Ukrainian drones can easily detect and target tanks, armored vehicles, and platoon-sized elements of soldiers. Once detected, these forces are attacked by multiple FPV drones and other Ukrainian fires. Russia has responded by shifting to small assault groups that are more difficult to detect. However, these smaller groups lack the combat power needed to overwhelm Ukrainian positions and capture terrain.

Russian Tactics During The Hannivka Assault

The recent Russian assault on Hannivka in late August provides insight into how Russian forces are attempting to overcome these drone defenses. According to the Russian MoD video describing this battle, Russian assault groups entered the settlement at night and during poor weather conditions. These conditions reduced the effectiveness of the smaller Ukrainian reconnaissance and FPV drones that normally detect approaching Russian forces. These drones generally lack night vision or thermal capabilities, while their small size makes them difficult to pilot in high winds. By avoiding detection, the Russian assault groups were able to reach Ukrainian positions before being detected.

Once the assault began, Ukrainian forces appeared to have called for drone support to counter the Russian forces. This support came primarily in the form of larger Baba Yaga bomber drones , which carry thermal imaging systems that allow them to operate at night. Furthermore, their larger size makes them more stable than smaller FPV drones in adverse weather conditions, although it also makes them easier targets.

Russian forces appeared to have anticipated the arrival of the Baba Yaga drones. They positioned their own FPV drone teams forward and employed what the Russian soldier described as the "waiter" tactic. Instead of searching for targets, Russian FPV drones waited for Ukrainian Baba Yagas to approach the area and then intercepted them. Positioning the Russian operators closer to the front reduced their flight time and limited the effects of electronic warfare on their drones. The interviewed soldier claims that the unit destroyed 792 Baba Yagas during the assault.

With the Ukrainian heavy bombers unable to reach the assault area, Russian ground forces could continue advancing and clear Ukrainian positions within the settlement. Earlier training videos posted by the Russian MoD show Russian forces training to clear urban areas. They follow doctrinal assault approaches, moving dismounted in small groups in a smooth, continuous pattern. The settlement was likely abandoned by civilians, which made it easier to clear. According to the Russian soldier in the interview, the assault groups made an effort to clear every room, including basements, to find Ukrainian defensive positions and drone operators.

While the video only covers the assault, Russian forces had spent weeks setting the stage for the operation. An earlier video posted by the MoD shows a montage of Russian drone and artillery strikes on Hannivka. These strikes systematically targeted obstacles and protective measures emplaced throughout the town. Russian drones also provided intelligence on the approximate locations of Ukrainian defensive positions. This preparatory work allowed the assault force to move quickly once the operation began.

However, the Russian account should be treated with caution. The Russian MoD has come under criticism in recent months for making bold claims about capturing settlements that remain contested or under Ukrainian control. There have also been reports suggesting that the Russian military bloggers have altered imagery to show battlefield success in areas where Russian forces have not made significant gains. Regardless, the video posted by the Russian MoD provides insight into the current assault and drone tactics being employed by Russian forces.

The Ukrainian Response To The New Russian Tactics

It is important to note that Hannivka is a relatively small village with a pre-war population of approximately 1,100 people. The village does not have any large buildings, and the surrounding terrain is generally flat. According to the Russian account, its primary significance was its location along a logistics corridor being used by Ukrainian forces. While this approach could work in a smaller village, it is unlikely to be as effective in a significantly larger settlement. It is also unlikely to produce the type of breakthrough that Russia has sought throughout its current offensive. Despite these limitations, these emerging Russian tactics are still important given the large number of small settlements that Russia must capture to gain control of the remainder of Donetsk Oblast.

As seen throughout the war, Ukraine will counter with new techniques and technologies. This will likely include autonomous systems that are less dependent on weather and visibility, including ground sensors and robots that can detect approaching Russian forces. Ukrainian forces may also find new methods to improve their drone capabilities at night and during inclement weather. They may also add additional obstacles and protections around forward positions to slow Russian assault groups and provide more time for Ukrainian forces to respond.

The reported Hannivka assault represents another step in the continuing tactical competition between Russian assault forces and Ukrainian drone operators. Rather than defeating Ukraine's drone network outright, the Russian approach attempts to exploit temporary weaknesses in that network and prevent heavier drones from responding. Its longer-term success will depend on whether Russia can repeat these tactics faster than Ukraine can adapt its defenses.

articles.title: Saharanpur mosque demolition: 'Why action at 5am?' Owaisi, Akhilesh question UP govt
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: AIMIM chief Asaduddin Owaisi and Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav on Saturday questioned the Uttar Pradesh government over the early-mo.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: AIMIM chief Asaduddin Owaisi and Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav on Saturday questioned the Uttar Pradesh government over the early-morning demolition of an allegedly illegal mosque inside the Saharanpur district collectorate complex."The fact that they cordoned off the area and demolished the mosque at 5am proves that the BJP's Yogi government did not want the matter to reach a higher court because they were in the wrong... This demonstrates that the BJP, the prime minister, and the chief minister of Uttar Pradesh harbour a hatred for the very word 'mosque'. That is why the mere sight of a mosque triggers fear in their hearts and minds... The BJP government in Uttar Pradesh and the BJP party itself are effectively dismantling the constitutional guarantee of freedom of religion specifically for Muslims," news agency ANI quoted Owaisi saying.Assuring legal assistance to the mosque authorities, Owaisi said, "If Yogi Adityanath and the BJP believe they will gain electoral advantage by flouting the law and conspiring to tear the Constitution to shreds, by trampling upon fundamental rights, they are mistaken... I appeal to the mosque's management committee to approach the high court or the Supreme Court. We stand ready to provide any legal assistance required... Divine justice will prevail, and they will have to pay the price for this, both constitutionally and legally."SP MP Akhilesh Yadav also questioned the government's decision, arguing that the matter could have been challenged before a higher court."Could justice not have been found in the high court? Could they not have appealed to the Supreme Court? Officials colluded at the government's behest to execute this action specifically to prevent them from securing justice in a higher court... You are snatching away people's right to justice; that is why I said there are only a hundred days left," he said."Those who do not respect other religions can never be Sanatanis. Those who trifle with the faith of others can never be Sanatanis. A true Hindu can never insult another; this is what we have learned in 'Sanatan Dharma'... True Sanatanis are people who cherish harmony; harmony should be the government's highest priority. Can anyone tell me why this is happening? It is happening because they were caught stealing funds meant for Lord Shri Ram... Everyone knows that members of the BJP were implicated. The move to form an SIT and send people to jail stripped them of their cover; the public now realizes what kind of people they are. That is why they are deliberately giving it a communal angle," he added.The mosque was demolished early Saturday after a district court on September 2 rejected the mosque committee’s appeal against an earlier demolition order. The collectorate complex was turned into a fortress for the operation, with all five entrances closed and the general public, including lawyers, barred from entering.Five companies of the Provincial Armed Constabulary and Rapid Action Force personnel were deployed at the site, while police conducted foot patrols and flag marches in sensitive areas to prevent any untoward incident.According to officials, the structure was declared illegal by the Saharanpur city magistrate on July 16, 2026, following a petition filed in 2025 by Bajrang Dal regional convener Vikas Tyagi. The mosque committee subsequently challenged the order before the district court, which rejected its appeal on September 2.Saharanpur Range DIG Abhishek Singh said the demolition cleared government land of encroachment and appealed to people to maintain peace and ignore rumours.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: LeT terrorist killed in J&K: Yasir was behind 2024 attack on IAF convoy, civilians
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Lashkar terrorist Yasir, a Pakistani national linked to Hafiz Saeed's outift, was killed by security forces in the higher reaches of Yusmar.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Lashkar terrorist Yasir, a Pakistani national linked to Hafiz Saeed's outift, was killed by security forces in the higher reaches of Yusmarg in central Kashmir, on Saturday.He was suspected of being involved in several major terror attacks in Jammu and Kashmir in 2024, including the ambush of an Indian Air Force convoy in Poonch and the killing of soldiers and civilian workers near Gulmarg.Yasir was gunned down on Friday during Operation Ashdar, launched after security forces received intelligence about the movement of a group of terrorists through the Pir Panjal mountains. Jammu and Kashmir Police identified the slain terrorist as Yasir and said he was affiliated with the banned Lashkar-e-Taiba (LeT).The police also posted a message on X after the operation, saying, "You Can Run But You Can't Hide!"Yasir's role in the 2024 attacksSecurity agencies had first detected Yasir's presence in the region in 2024. Officials said intelligence inputs pointed to his involvement in at least three major terror attacks that year.The first was the ambush of an IAF convoy in Poonch on May 4, 2024. Terrorists opened fire on the convoy near Shahsitar in the Surankote area as the personnel were returning to their base at Sanai Top. One IAF member was killed and four others were injured.Yasir was also suspected of involvement in the October 20 attack at Gangangir near Sonamarg, where terrorists killed seven people, including a local doctor.Four days later, on October 24, terrorists attacked an Army vehicle in Bota Pathri near Gulmarg. The attack killed five people, including three soldiers and two civilian porters. Officials said Yasir was part of the group behind the attack.Link to Lashkar Yasir was reportedly operating with a Lashkar-e-Taiba group led by commander Junai Ahmed Bhat. Bhat was killed by security forces in the Dachigam forest on the outskirts of Srinagar on December 3, 2024.After the Bota Pathri attack, Yasir and another Lashkar terrorist, identified as Musa, are believed to have remained hidden in the Yusmarg and Pulwama areas. Officials said they later crossed to the Jammu side of the Pir Panjal range before returning to the Valley earlier this month.How Yasir was tracked downThe latest operation began after security forces tracked the movement of the terrorist group from Ashdar Gali in Poonch towards Pakherpora in Pulwama through Yusmarg.The Army, J&K Police and CRPF established a cordon in the area on September 1. They made contact with the terrorists on September 3 at Ashdar Gali, a remote mountain ridge. Yasir was eventually killed in the exchange of fire. An AK rifle was recovered from the site.The operation is still continuing as security forces search for Musa, who is believed to be hiding among large boulders and natural caves. The encounter site lies between 12,000 and 15,500 feet in the Pir Panjal range, where heavy rain and visibility of as little as five metres have made the operation particularly difficult.Get the latest India News and Live updates.
